title: Routine Work, Firm Boundaries, and the Rise of Local Supplier Entry
summary: This paper examines why U.S. business applications rose 40% between 2005-2019 while conversion to employer firms fell by nearly half. The authors find that boundary redrawing (outsourcing routine-cognitive work) creates demand for domestic specialist suppliers. A one percentage-point higher baseline routine employment share raises applications by 27.8 per 100,000 residents, with entry concentrating in micro-establishments.
key_points: Between 2005 and 2019, U.S. business applications rose 40 percent while conversion to employer firms fell by nearly half
Routine-cognitive work can be governed through deliverables and thinner buyer/supplier interfaces
When place-bound routine work is outsourced, it creates demand for domestic specialist suppliers
Across 722 commuting zones, a one percentage-point higher baseline routine employment share raises applications by 27.8 per 100,000 residents
Realized entry concentrates in micro-establishments with no observed startup quality gains
Evidence points to local supplier entry rather than routine-manual displacement as the mechanism
why_it_matters: This research documents a structural shift in how work is organized in the U.S. economy, specifically how routine tasks are being unbundled from firms and delegated to local suppliers. While not a direct market structure or macro catalyst paper, it provides empirical context for understanding long-term changes in business formation patterns.
important_numbers: near 50% decrease in conversion to employer firms
27.8 applications per 100,000 residents (per 1 percentage-point increase in routine employment share)
